questions.question: Which of the following is the contrapositive of the statement "If Gandalf has come to the Shire, then there will be fireworks."?
questions.answer: The contrapositive of "if $P$ then $Q$" is "if not $Q$ then not $P$": if there are no fireworks, then Gandalf has not come to the Shire.
options: If there are fireworks, then Gandalf has come to the Shire.
If there are not fireworks, then Gandalf has not come to the Shire.
If Gandalf does not come to the Shire there will be no fireworks.
Gandalf has come to the Shire and there are no fireworks

questions.question: Which one of the following is NOT a primitive of $\displaystyle\int \frac{\sin^3 x+\cos^3 x}{\sin x+\cos x}\,dx$ ?
questions.answer:
Using $a^3+b^3=(a+b)(a^2-ab+b^2)$, the integrand is $\sin^2x-\sin x\cos x+\cos^2x = 1-\sin x\cos x = 1-\tfrac12\sin 2x$.

Differentiating each option: (A) $1-\tfrac12\sin 2x$ ✓; (B) $1-\tfrac12\cos 2x$ ✗; (C) $1-\sin x\cos x$ ✓; (D) $1-\sin x\cos x$ ✓. So (B) is not a primitive.

questions.question: What is the negation of the statement $\forall x\in\mathbb{Z},\ \exists y\in\mathbb{Z},\ y\ge x$ ?
questions.answer: Negating a quantified statement swaps $\forall\leftrightarrow\exists$ and negates the final condition: $\neg(y\ge x)$ is $y<x$. So the negation is $\exists x\in\mathbb{Z},\ \forall y\in\mathbb{Z},\ y<x$.

questions.question: Given the vector $\overrightarrow{OP}=\sqrt2\,\mathbf{i}-\mathbf{j}+\mathbf{k}$, this vector
questions.answer: $|\overrightarrow{OP}|=\sqrt{2+1+1}=2$. The angles with the axes satisfy $\cos\alpha=\dfrac{\sqrt2}{2}$, $\cos\beta=-\dfrac12$, $\cos\gamma=\dfrac12$, so $\alpha=45^\circ$, $\beta=120^\circ$, $\gamma=60^\circ$. This is option (B).
options: makes an angle of $120^\circ$ with the positive $y$-axis and $30^\circ$ with the positive $z$-axis.
makes an angle of $45^\circ$ with the positive $x$-axis and $120^\circ$ with the positive $y$-axis.
makes an angle of $45^\circ$ with the positive $x$-axis and $150^\circ$ with the positive $y$-axis.
makes an angle of $135^\circ$ with the positive $x$-axis and $150^\circ$ with the positive $y$-axis.

questions.question: Evaluate the complex number $\left(-2+2i\sqrt3\right)^3$.
questions.answer: $-2+2i\sqrt3 = 4\left(\cos\tfrac{2\pi}{3}+i\sin\tfrac{2\pi}{3}\right)$. By de Moivre's theorem its cube is $4^3\left(\cos 2\pi+i\sin 2\pi\right)=64$.

questions.question:
A particle of mass $m$ kg is on a smooth inclined plane that makes an angle $\theta$ with the horizontal. The particle is attached to a light inextensible string that passes over a smooth pulley at the top of the plane. The other end of the string is connected to a hanging particle of mass $M$ kg. The system is released from rest and moves without friction (the hanging mass moves down). Assume the string remains taut, the acceleration of both masses is $a$, and gravity is $g$.

Which of the following pairs of equations correctly represents the motion of the two masses?
questions.answer: The hanging mass moves down: $Mg-T=Ma$. The mass on the plane is pulled up the slope by $T$ against the component of its weight along the slope, $mg\sin\theta$: $T-mg\sin\theta=ma$. This is option (D).

questions.question: Which graph matches the parametric equations $x=2\cos 5t,\ y=2\sin 2t$ ?
questions.answer: The curve is closed with period $2\pi$. It touches the vertical sides $x=\pm2$ when $\cos 5t=\pm1$, i.e. at $t=\tfrac{k\pi}{5}$: that is 5 touching points on each side (at five different heights). It touches the top and bottom $y=\pm2$ when $\sin 2t=\pm1$: only 2 touching points on each of the top and bottom. The graph with 5 lobes on each side and 2 on the top/bottom is (C).

questions.question: The polynomial equation $P(z)=0$ has exactly one complex (non-real) coefficient. Three of the roots of this equation are $z=4+2i$, $z=-9-2i$ and $z=0$. The minimum degree of $P(z)$ is
questions.answer:
Since $P$ has non-real coefficients, the conjugate root theorem does not force $4-2i$ or $-9+2i$ to be roots. Try the cubic with just these three roots:
$$P(z)=z\,(z-4-2i)(z+9+2i)=z^3+5z^2-(32+26i)z,$$
since the sum of the roots is $(4+2i)+(-9-2i)+0=-5$ and $(4+2i)(-9-2i)=-32-26i$. Its coefficients are $1,\,5,\,-(32+26i),\,0$, so exactly one coefficient ($-32-26i$) is non-real. At least 3 roots are needed, so the minimum degree is 3.

questions.question:
There are 4 trolls on a bridge. Each troll is either a knight (always tells the truth) or a knave (always lies). Each troll can see the other three trolls.

- Troll 1: "Every troll can see at least 1 knave."
- Troll 2: "I can see at least 1 troll that can only see knaves."
- Troll 3: "All trolls are afraid of goats."
- Troll 4: "Some trolls are afraid of goats."

What can be deduced?
questions.answer:
*Troll 1 is a knight.* If Troll 1 were a knave, then some troll sees no knave, and the only troll who can fail to see a knave is Troll 1 itself (every other troll sees Troll 1). So Trolls 2, 3, 4 would all be knights; but then Troll 2's statement is false (nobody sees only knaves), contradiction.

*Troll 2 is a knave.* Every troll sees a knave, so there are at least 2 knaves. If Troll 2 were a knight, some troll would see only knaves; the only possibility is Troll 1 seeing Trolls 2, 3, 4 all knaves, contradicting Troll 2 being a knight. So Troll 2 is a knave, and (his statement being false) Troll 1 does not see only knaves, so not all of Trolls 2, 3, 4 are knaves. With at least two knaves, exactly one of Trolls 3 and 4 is a knave.

*Troll 3 is the knave.* If Troll 3 were a knight, "all are afraid" would be true, so "some are afraid" would be true and Troll 4 would be a knight too, leaving only one knave, a contradiction. So Troll 3 is a knave and Troll 4 a knight.

Troll 4 tells the truth: some trolls are afraid of goats (and Troll 3 lies, so not all are). The answer is (C).
options: No trolls are afraid of goats
Some trolls are afraid of goats
All trolls are afraid of goats

questions.question: The line $\mathbf{r}_1(t)=\begin{pmatrix}4\\-2\\0\end{pmatrix}+t\begin{pmatrix}\lambda\\1\\2\end{pmatrix}$ intersects the sphere $\left|\mathbf{r}_2-\begin{pmatrix}1\\-2\\3\end{pmatrix}\right|=3$ at exactly one point. Which one of the following is correct?
questions.answer:
The line meets the sphere at exactly one point when it is tangent. Substitute $\mathbf{r}_1(t)$ into the sphere equation: $\begin{pmatrix}3+\lambda t\\ t\\ 2t-3\end{pmatrix}$ has squared length $9$:
$$(3+\lambda t)^2+t^2+(2t-3)^2=9\ \Rightarrow\ (\lambda^2+5)t^2+(6\lambda-12)t+9=0.$$
One solution requires the discriminant to be zero: $(6\lambda-12)^2-36(\lambda^2+5)=0$, i.e. $-144\lambda-36=0$, so $\lambda=-\tfrac14$. (The tangent point has $t=\tfrac43$, so $t$ is not one of the options.)

questions.question: Let $z=1+3i$ and $w=2-6i$. Find $\overline{z}+w$ in modulus-argument form.
questions.answer:
$\overline z+w=(1-3i)+(2-6i)=3-9i$.

Modulus: $\sqrt{9+81}=3\sqrt{10}$. Argument: $\tan^{-1}(-3)$ (fourth quadrant), i.e. $-\tan^{-1}3\approx-1.249$.

$$\overline z+w=3\sqrt{10}\left[\cos\left(\tan^{-1}(-3)\right)+i\sin\left(\tan^{-1}(-3)\right)\right]$$

questions.question: Let $z=1+3i$ and $w=2-6i$. Write $\dfrac zw$ in the form $x+iy$, where $x$ and $y$ are real numbers.
If the points $A(0,1,1)$, $B(2,5,9)$ and $C(3,b,c)$ are collinear, find the values of $b$ and $c$.
questions.answer: $\overrightarrow{AB}=\begin{pmatrix}2\\4\\8\end{pmatrix}$ and $\overrightarrow{BC}=\begin{pmatrix}1\\b-5\\c-9\end{pmatrix}$. For collinear points $\overrightarrow{BC}=k\overrightarrow{AB}$; comparing the $x$-components, $k=\tfrac12$. Then $b-5=2\Rightarrow b=7$ and $c-9=4\Rightarrow c=13$.

questions.question: Prove that if $n\in\mathbb{Z}$, then $n^2+2$ is not divisible by $4$.
questions.answer:
Every integer is even or odd.

*Case 1:* $n=2k$. Then $n^2+2=4k^2+2$. Since $4k^2$ is divisible by 4 and $2$ is not, $n^2+2$ is not divisible by 4.

*Case 2:* $n=2k+1$. Then $n^2+2=4k^2+4k+3$, which leaves remainder $3$ on division by 4.

In both cases $n^2+2$ is not divisible by 4. $\blacksquare$

questions.question: Find $\displaystyle\int\frac{-x-17}{x^2-x-6}\,dx$.
Given $\mathbf{a}=\mathbf{i}-\mathbf{j}+2\mathbf{k}$ and $\mathbf{b}=\mathbf{i}-2\mathbf{j}+3\mathbf{k}$, find the angle between the two vectors to the nearest degree.
questions.answer:
$\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf b=1+2+6=9$, $|\mathbf a|=\sqrt{1+1+4}=\sqrt6$, $|\mathbf b|=\sqrt{1+4+9}=\sqrt{14}$.

$$\cos\theta=\frac{9}{\sqrt6\sqrt{14}}=\frac{9}{\sqrt{84}}\ \Rightarrow\ \theta\approx10.89^\circ\approx11^\circ.$$

(The paper's solution wrote $\mathbf a$ as $(1,-1,2)$ but its working line for $|\mathbf a|$ showed $4+1+1$; the value $\sqrt6$ and the answer $11^\circ$ are correct.)

questions.question: By using the contrapositive, prove that if $a$ and $b$ are integers and $a+b\ge15$, then either $a\ge7$ or $b\ge8$.
questions.answer:
The contrapositive is: if $a<7$ and $b<8$, then $a+b<15$.

Suppose $a<7$ and $b<8$. Since $a,b$ are integers, $a\le6$ and $b\le7$, so $a+b\le13<15$. (Even without integrality, $a+b<7+8=15$.) The contrapositive is true, and an implication is logically equivalent to its contrapositive, so the original statement is true. $\blacksquare$

questions.question:
A line $L$ has vector equation $\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\\3\end{pmatrix}+\lambda\begin{pmatrix}2\\-1\\1\end{pmatrix}$, $\lambda\in\mathbb{R}$. The point $A$ has position vector $\mathbf a=\begin{pmatrix}5\\1\\0\end{pmatrix}$. Let $\mathbf r_0=\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\\3\end{pmatrix}$ be the position vector of a point on $L$.

Find the projection of $\mathbf a-\mathbf r_0$ onto the line (that is, onto the direction vector of $L$).
questions.answer:
$\mathbf a-\mathbf r_0=\begin{pmatrix}4\\-1\\-3\end{pmatrix}$, $\mathbf d=\begin{pmatrix}2\\-1\\1\end{pmatrix}$.
$$\operatorname{proj}_{\mathbf d}(\mathbf a-\mathbf r_0)=\frac{(\mathbf a-\mathbf r_0)\cdot\mathbf d}{|\mathbf d|^2}\mathbf d=\frac{8+1-3}{4+1+1}\begin{pmatrix}2\\-1\\1\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}2\\-1\\1\end{pmatrix}.$$

questions.question:
A line $L$ has vector equation $\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\\3\end{pmatrix}+\lambda\begin{pmatrix}2\\-1\\1\end{pmatrix}$, $\lambda\in\mathbb{R}$, and $A$ has position vector $\begin{pmatrix}5\\1\\0\end{pmatrix}$. The projection of $\overrightarrow{CA}$ onto $L$, where $C=(1,2,3)$ lies on $L$, is $\begin{pmatrix}2\\-1\\1\end{pmatrix}$.

Hence find the point at which the perpendicular from $A$ to $L$ meets $L$.
questions.answer: The foot of the perpendicular $B$ satisfies $\overrightarrow{CB}=\operatorname{proj}=\begin{pmatrix}2\\-1\\1\end{pmatrix}$, so $\overrightarrow{OB}=\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\\3\end{pmatrix}+\begin{pmatrix}2\\-1\\1\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}3\\1\\4\end{pmatrix}$. The point is $B(3,1,4)$ (it corresponds to $\lambda=1$).

questions.question:
A line $L$ passes through $(1,2,3)$ with direction $\begin{pmatrix}2\\-1\\1\end{pmatrix}$, and $A=(5,1,0)$. The perpendicular from $A$ meets $L$ at $B(3,1,4)$.

Find the shortest distance from $A$ to $L$.
questions.answer: The shortest distance is $AB=\sqrt{(5-3)^2+(1-1)^2+(0-4)^2}=\sqrt{4+16}=2\sqrt5$ units.

questions.question: Prove or disprove: there exists an integer $k$ for which the expression $\dfrac{(1+i)^k}{(1-i)^{k-1}}$ is purely real or purely imaginary.
questions.answer:
In polar form $1+i=\sqrt2\,\mathrm{cis}\tfrac\pi4$ and $1-i=\sqrt2\,\mathrm{cis}\left(-\tfrac\pi4\right)$. By de Moivre's theorem
$$\frac{(1+i)^k}{(1-i)^{k-1}}=\frac{2^{k/2}\,\mathrm{cis}\tfrac{k\pi}{4}}{2^{(k-1)/2}\,\mathrm{cis}\left(-\tfrac{(k-1)\pi}{4}\right)}=\sqrt2\,\mathrm{cis}\,\frac{(2k-1)\pi}{4}.$$
The argument $\dfrac{(2k-1)\pi}{4}$ is an odd multiple of $\dfrac\pi4$, so it is never a multiple of $\dfrac\pi2$ (that would need $2k-1$ to be even). Hence the expression is never real and never purely imaginary: it cycles through $1+i,\,-1+i,\,-1-i,\,1-i$ as $k=1,2,3,4$ and then repeats.

So there is **no** such integer $k$ (the statement is disproved).

questions.question: Find $\displaystyle\int\frac{\tan 2x}{1+\cos 2x}\,dx$.
questions.answer:
*Method 1.* Let $t=\tan x$, so $dx=\dfrac{dt}{1+t^2}$, $\tan2x=\dfrac{2t}{1-t^2}$, $1+\cos2x=\dfrac{2}{1+t^2}$.
$$\int\frac{\frac{2t}{1-t^2}}{\frac{2}{1+t^2}}\cdot\frac{dt}{1+t^2}=\int\frac{t}{1-t^2}\,dt=-\frac12\ln|1-t^2|+C=-\frac12\ln\left|1-\tan^2x\right|+C.$$

*Method 2.* With $u=\cos 2x$, $\tan 2x\,dx=-\dfrac{du}{2u}$, giving $-\dfrac12\displaystyle\int\frac{du}{u(1+u)}=-\dfrac12\ln\left|\dfrac{\cos2x}{1+\cos2x}\right|+C$, which differs from Method 1 only by a constant.

questions.question: The velocity $v$ m/s of a particle moving in simple harmonic motion along the $x$-axis is given by $v^2=-4x^2+96x+20$. Find the acceleration of the particle in terms of $x$.
questions.answer: $\ddot x=\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\tfrac12v^2\right)=\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(-2x^2+48x+10\right)=-4x+48$.

questions.question: A particle moves in simple harmonic motion along the $x$-axis with $v^2=-4x^2+96x+20$ and acceleration $\ddot x=-4x+48$. State the period and the centre of the motion.
questions.answer: $\ddot x=-4(x-12)$, which has the form $-n^2(x-c)$ with $n^2=4$, $c=12$. The centre of motion is $x=12$ and the period is $\dfrac{2\pi}{n}=\dfrac{2\pi}{2}=\pi$ seconds.

questions.question: A particle moves in simple harmonic motion along the $x$-axis with $v^2=-4x^2+96x+20$ and centre of motion $x=12$. What is the maximum speed of the particle?
questions.answer: Maximum speed occurs at the centre $x=12$: $v^2=-4(144)+96(12)+20=-576+1152+20=596$. Maximum speed $=\sqrt{596}=2\sqrt{149}$ m/s.

questions.question: Sketch on an Argand diagram the set of all points $z$ satisfying $\arg\left(\dfrac{z-2}{z+2}\right)=\dfrac\pi4$, showing all important features.
questions.answer:
$\arg\dfrac{z-2}{z+2}=\arg(z-2)-\arg(z+2)$ is the angle subtended at $z$ by the interval joining $-2$ and $2$. The locus is therefore an arc of a circle through $-2$ and $2$, lying in the upper half-plane.

A chord of length 4 subtending an inscribed angle $\tfrac\pi4$ on the major arc means a central angle of $\tfrac\pi2$, so the radius is $\dfrac{4}{2\sin(\pi/4)}=2\sqrt2$ and the centre is $(0,2)$. The sketch is the **major arc** of the circle $|z-2i|=2\sqrt2$ lying above the real axis, from $-2$ to $2$, with highest point $z=(2+2\sqrt2)i$. The end points $z=\pm2$ are excluded (open circles).

questions.question: Sketch on an Argand diagram the set of all points $z$ satisfying $\arg\left(\dfrac{z-2}{z+2}\right)=\dfrac\pi2$, showing all important features.
questions.answer: Here the interval from $-2$ to $2$ subtends a right angle at $z$, so by the angle in a semicircle the locus is the **upper semicircle** of $|z|=2$ (centre $0$, radius $2$, highest point $2i$), with the end points $\pm2$ excluded.

questions.question: Sketch on an Argand diagram the region where $\dfrac\pi4\le\arg\left(\dfrac{z-2}{z+2}\right)\le\dfrac\pi2$.
questions.answer: The region lies between the two loci: it is the part of the upper half-plane **outside the semicircle** $|z|=2$ and **inside (or on) the major arc** of the circle $|z-2i|=2\sqrt2$ (excluding the points $\pm2$). Points inside the semicircle have argument greater than $\tfrac\pi2$, and points outside the large arc have argument less than $\tfrac\pi4$, so the shaded region is the crescent-shaped area between the two arcs, including both boundary arcs.

questions.question: Find the exact value of $\displaystyle\int_1^e\left[\ln x\right]^2dx$.
questions.answer:
Integrate by parts twice. $\displaystyle\int(\ln x)^2dx=x(\ln x)^2-\int 2\ln x\,dx=x(\ln x)^2-2\left(x\ln x-x\right)+C$.
$$\int_1^e(\ln x)^2dx=\Big[x(\ln x)^2-2x\ln x+2x\Big]_1^e=(e-2e+2e)-(2)=e-2.$$

questions.question: The curve $y=\ln x$ on the interval $[1,e]$ is rotated about the $x$-axis. Find the exact volume of the solid generated.
questions.answer: $$V=\pi\int_1^e y^2\,dx=\pi\int_1^e(\ln x)^2dx=\pi(e-2)\ \text{units}^3.$$

questions.question:
A monic polynomial of degree 4 has integer coefficients and two real integer roots. Which of the following could be a root of the polynomial? Justify your answer.
$$\frac{1+\sqrt{11}\,i}{2},\qquad 1+\frac i2,\qquad \frac12+i,\qquad \frac{1+\sqrt{13}\,i}{2}$$
questions.answer:
The polynomial has real coefficients, so a non-real root $\alpha$ and its conjugate $\bar\alpha$ are both roots. Dividing out the two integer-root linear factors (monic, integer) leaves a monic quadratic with integer coefficients, namely $x^2-(\alpha+\bar\alpha)x+\alpha\bar\alpha$. So we need both $\alpha+\bar\alpha=2\operatorname{Re}\alpha$ and $|\alpha|^2$ to be integers.

- $\dfrac{1+\sqrt{11}i}{2}$: sum $=1$, product $=\dfrac{1+11}{4}=3$. Quadratic $x^2-x+3$: all integers ✓.
- $1+\dfrac i2$: sum $=2$, product $=1+\tfrac14=\tfrac54$ ✗.
- $\dfrac12+i$: sum $=1$, product $=\tfrac14+1=\tfrac54$ ✗.
- $\dfrac{1+\sqrt{13}i}{2}$: sum $=1$, product $=\dfrac{1+13}{4}=\tfrac72$ ✗.

Only $\dfrac{1+\sqrt{11}\,i}{2}$ could be a root.

questions.question: Determine the coordinates of the point which divides the line segment joining $(1,-2,3)$ and $(3,4,-5)$ externally in the ratio $2:3$.
questions.answer:
Let $A=(1,-2,3)$, $B=(3,4,-5)$ and let $C$ divide $AB$ externally in the ratio $2:3$, i.e. $AC:CB=2:3$ with $C$ outside the segment, beyond $A$. Then $\overrightarrow{AC}=-\tfrac23\overrightarrow{CB}$, so the section formula with ratio $2:-3$ applies:
$$\overrightarrow{OC}=\frac{3\overrightarrow{OA}-2\overrightarrow{OB}}{3-2}=3\begin{pmatrix}1\\-2\\3\end{pmatrix}-2\begin{pmatrix}3\\4\\-5\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}-3\\-14\\19\end{pmatrix}.$$
The point is $(-3,-14,19)$.

(Check: $\overrightarrow{CA}=(4,12,-16)$ and $\overrightarrow{CB}=(6,18,-24)$ point the same way from $C$ and $CA:CB=2:3$, so $C$ lies outside the segment $AB$.)

questions.question: Let $x,y,z$ be positive real numbers with $xy+yz+zx=1$. Prove that $10x^2+10y^2+z^2\ge4$.
questions.answer:
Since $xy+yz+zx=1$, we have $4=4(xy+yz+zx)$, so
$$10x^2+10y^2+z^2-4=10x^2+10y^2+z^2-4xy-4yz-4zx.$$
Now $(2x+2y-z)^2=4x^2+4y^2+z^2+8xy-4xz-4yz$, and subtracting gives
$$10x^2+10y^2+z^2-4xy-4yz-4zx=(2x+2y-z)^2+6x^2+6y^2-12xy=(2x+2y-z)^2+6(x-y)^2\ge0.$$
Hence $10x^2+10y^2+z^2\ge4$. $\blacksquare$

(The paper's working wrote the first bracket as $(2x+2y-4)^2$; it should read $(2x+2y-z)^2$.)

questions.question:
Two birds fly along straight paths with vector equations
$$\mathbf r_1=\begin{pmatrix}-1\\5\\2\end{pmatrix}+\lambda\begin{pmatrix}2\\a\\0\end{pmatrix},\qquad \mathbf r_2=\begin{pmatrix}4\\-1\\3\end{pmatrix}+\mu\begin{pmatrix}0\\1\\-1\end{pmatrix},$$
where $\lambda$ and $\mu$ are scalar parameters. The angle between the flight paths is $120^\circ$. Find the value of $a$.
questions.answer:
Directions $\mathbf d_1=(2,a,0)$, $\mathbf d_2=(0,1,-1)$: $\mathbf d_1\cdot\mathbf d_2=a$, $|\mathbf d_1|=\sqrt{4+a^2}$, $|\mathbf d_2|=\sqrt2$.
$$a=\sqrt{4+a^2}\,\sqrt2\cos120^\circ=-\frac{\sqrt2}{2}\sqrt{4+a^2}.$$
So $a<0$. Squaring: $a^2=\tfrac12(4+a^2)\Rightarrow a^2=4$, so $a=-2$ (reject $a=2$ since $\cos120^\circ<0$).

questions.question:
Two birds fly along straight paths with vector equations
$$\mathbf r_1=\begin{pmatrix}-1\\5\\2\end{pmatrix}+\lambda\begin{pmatrix}2\\-2\\0\end{pmatrix},\qquad \mathbf r_2=\begin{pmatrix}4\\-1\\3\end{pmatrix}+\mu\begin{pmatrix}0\\1\\-1\end{pmatrix}.$$
Determine whether the flight paths will meet, and if so, where.
questions.answer:
Equate components: $-1+2\lambda=4$, $5-2\lambda=-1+\mu$, $2=3-\mu$.

The first gives $\lambda=\tfrac52$ and the third gives $\mu=1$. Check the second: $5-5=0$ and $-1+1=0$ ✓. The equations are consistent, so the paths meet, at $\lambda=\tfrac52$, $\mu=1$:
$$(x,y,z)=(4,\,0,\,2).$$

questions.question:
Let $z$ be a solution of $z^7-1=0$ with $z\ne1$. Compute the numerical value of
$$z^{10}+\frac1{z^{10}}+z^{30}+\frac1{z^{30}}+z^{50}+\frac1{z^{50}}.$$
Find the greatest value of the moduli of the complex numbers $z$ satisfying the equation $\left|z-\dfrac4z\right|=2$.
questions.answer:
Let $|z|=r$. By the triangle inequality,
$$r=|z|=\left|\left(z-\frac4z\right)+\frac4z\right|\le\left|z-\frac4z\right|+\frac4{r}=2+\frac4r.$$
So $r^2-2r-4\le0$, giving $r\le1+\sqrt5$.

This bound is attained: for the real number $z=1+\sqrt5$ we have $z-\dfrac4z=z-(\sqrt5-1)=2$, which satisfies the equation. (Alternatively, $z^4-12z^2+16=0$ gives $z^2=6\pm2\sqrt5$ and $\sqrt{6+2\sqrt5}=1+\sqrt5$.)

The greatest value of $|z|$ is $1+\sqrt5$.

questions.question:
A particle of mass $m$ and positive charge $q$ moves along the $x$-axis under the influence of a spatially varying electric potential $P(x)=-A\sin^2x$, where $A>0$ and $\tfrac\pi6\le x\le\tfrac\pi2$. The electric force on the particle is $\vec F=q\vec E$, where the electric field is $\vec E=-\dfrac{dP}{dx}$.

Assuming the electric force is the only force acting on the particle, show that its acceleration is $a(x)=\dfrac{qA}{m}\sin(2x)$.
questions.answer: $E=-\dfrac{dP}{dx}=2A\sin x\cos x=A\sin2x$. By Newton's second law, $ma=qE=qA\sin2x$, so $a=\dfrac{qA}{m}\sin2x$. $\blacksquare$

questions.question:
A particle of mass $m$ and positive charge $q$ starts at $x=\dfrac\pi6$ with velocity $\sqrt{\dfrac{qA}{2m}}$ (in the positive $x$ direction) and moves along the $x$-axis with acceleration $a(x)=\dfrac{qA}{m}\sin2x$, for $\tfrac\pi6\le x\le\tfrac\pi2$, where $A>0$.

Hence show that the velocity of the particle at position $x$ is $v=\sqrt{\dfrac{2qA}{m}}\sin x$.
questions.answer:
$\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\tfrac12v^2\right)=a$, so $\dfrac d{dx}(v^2)=\dfrac{2qA}{m}\sin2x$ and $v^2=-\dfrac{qA}{m}\cos2x+C$.

At $x=\tfrac\pi6$, $v^2=\tfrac{qA}{2m}$: $\dfrac{qA}{2m}=-\dfrac{qA}{m}\cdot\dfrac12+C\Rightarrow C=\dfrac{qA}{m}$. So
$$v^2=\frac{qA}{m}(1-\cos2x)=\frac{2qA}{m}\sin^2x.$$
Since $a\ge0$ on the interval and the particle starts moving to the right, it keeps moving right, so $v>0$: $v=\sqrt{\dfrac{2qA}{m}}\sin x$. $\blacksquare$

(Alternatively, by conservation of energy, $\tfrac12mv^2+qP(x)$ is constant.)

questions.question: A particle moves along the $x$-axis, starting at $x=\dfrac\pi6$, with velocity $v=\sqrt{\dfrac{2qA}{m}}\sin x$ at position $x$ (where $q,A,m>0$). Find how much time it takes to reach $x=\dfrac\pi2$.
questions.answer:
$\dfrac{dx}{dt}=\sqrt{\dfrac{2qA}{m}}\sin x$, so
$$T=\sqrt{\frac m{2qA}}\int_{\pi/6}^{\pi/2}\frac{dx}{\sin x}=\sqrt{\frac m{2qA}}\Big[\ln\left|\tan\tfrac x2\right|\Big]_{\pi/6}^{\pi/2}=\sqrt{\frac m{2qA}}\left(\ln1-\ln\tan\tfrac\pi{12}\right).$$
(The antiderivative of $\operatorname{cosec}x$ can be obtained with $t=\tan\tfrac x2$ or by $\int\dfrac{\sin x}{1-\cos^2x}dx$.) Since $\tan\tfrac\pi{12}=2-\sqrt3$,
$$T=\sqrt{\frac m{2qA}}\ln\left(2+\sqrt3\right).$$

questions.question: Show that $\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/2}(\sin x)^{2k}\cos x\,dx=\frac1{2k+1}$, where $k$ is a positive integer.
questions.answer:
Let $u=\sin x$, $du=\cos x\,dx$; limits $0\to1$:
$$\int_0^1u^{2k}du=\left[\frac{u^{2k+1}}{2k+1}\right]_0^1=\frac1{2k+1}.\ \blacksquare$$

questions.question:
Given that $\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/2}(\sin x)^{2k}\cos x\,dx=\frac1{2k+1}$ for non-negative integers $k$, show that
$$\int_0^{\pi/2}(\cos x)^{2n+1}dx=\sum_{k=0}^n\frac{(-1)^k}{2k+1}\binom nk .$$
questions.answer:
Write $(\cos x)^{2n+1}=(\cos^2x)^n\cos x=(1-\sin^2x)^n\cos x$ and expand by the binomial theorem:
$$(1-\sin^2x)^n=\sum_{k=0}^n\binom nk(-1)^k(\sin x)^{2k}.$$
Therefore
$$\int_0^{\pi/2}(\cos x)^{2n+1}dx=\sum_{k=0}^n\binom nk(-1)^k\int_0^{\pi/2}(\sin x)^{2k}\cos x\,dx=\sum_{k=0}^n\frac{(-1)^k}{2k+1}\binom nk.\ \blacksquare$$

questions.question: Find $\displaystyle\int\frac{\sin x}{\sin x+\cos x+e^x}\,dx$.
questions.answer:
Let $I=\displaystyle\int\frac{\sin x}{S}dx$ and $J=\displaystyle\int\frac{\cos x+e^x}{S}dx$, where $S=\sin x+\cos x+e^x$. Then $I+J=\displaystyle\int\frac{S}{S}dx=x$.

Also $S'=\cos x-\sin x+e^x$, so $J-I=\displaystyle\int\frac{S'}{S}dx=\ln|S|$.

Subtracting, $2I=x-\ln|S|$, so
$$\int\frac{\sin x}{\sin x+\cos x+e^x}dx=\frac x2-\frac12\ln\left|\sin x+\cos x+e^x\right|+C.$$

questions.question:
Two stones are thrown simultaneously from the same point, in the same direction and with the same non-zero angle of projection $\alpha$ above the horizontal, but with different speeds $U$ and $V$ m/s, $U<V$. The slower stone lands at a point $P$ at the same level as the point of projection. At that instant the faster stone is just clearing a wall of height $h$ above the level of projection.

Show that, while both stones are in flight, the line joining the two stones has a constant inclination. Hence express the horizontal distance from $P$ to the wall in terms of $h$ and $\alpha$.
questions.answer:
Take the point of projection as the origin. At time $t$ (no air resistance) the stones are at
$$(Ut\cos\alpha,\ Ut\sin\alpha-\tfrac12gt^2)\quad\text{and}\quad(Vt\cos\alpha,\ Vt\sin\alpha-\tfrac12gt^2).$$
The gradient of the line joining them is
$$\frac{Vt\sin\alpha-Ut\sin\alpha}{Vt\cos\alpha-Ut\cos\alpha}=\tan\alpha,$$
which is constant, so the line always makes the angle $\alpha$ with the horizontal.

When the slower stone is at $P$ on the ground, the faster stone is at the top of the wall, at height $h$. The line from $P$ to that stone has inclination $\alpha$, so the horizontal distance from $P$ to the wall is $\dfrac h{\tan\alpha}=h\cot\alpha$.

questions.question:
Two stones are thrown simultaneously from the same point, in the same direction and at the same angle of projection $\alpha$ above the horizontal, with speeds $U$ and $V$ m/s, $U<V$. The slower stone lands at a point $P$ at the same level as the point of projection. At that instant the faster stone clears a wall, and its downward path makes an angle $\beta$ with the horizontal.

Show that $V(\tan\alpha+\tan\beta)=2U\tan\alpha$.
questions.answer:
The slower stone lands when $Ut\sin\alpha-\tfrac12gt^2=0$, $t\ne0$, i.e. $t=\dfrac{2U\sin\alpha}{g}$.

At this time the faster stone has velocity components $\dot x=V\cos\alpha$, $\dot y=V\sin\alpha-gt$. Its path is descending at angle $\beta$, so $\dfrac{\dot y}{\dot x}=-\tan\beta$:
$$\frac{V\sin\alpha-2U\sin\alpha}{V\cos\alpha}=-\tan\beta\ \Rightarrow\ V\tan\alpha-2U\tan\alpha=-V\tan\beta,$$
so $V(\tan\alpha+\tan\beta)=2U\tan\alpha$. $\blacksquare$

questions.question:
Let $I_n=\displaystyle\int_1^e x(\ln x)^n\,dx$, where $n\ge0$ is an integer. Show that
$$I_{n+1}=\frac12e^2-\frac12(n+1)I_n.$$
questions.answer:
Integrate by parts with $u=(\ln x)^{n+1}$, $dv=x\,dx$, so $du=(n+1)(\ln x)^n\dfrac1x\,dx$ and $v=\dfrac{x^2}2$:
$$I_{n+1}=\left[\frac{x^2}2(\ln x)^{n+1}\right]_1^e-\frac{n+1}2\int_1^ex(\ln x)^n\,dx=\frac{e^2}2-\frac{n+1}2I_n.\ \blacksquare$$

questions.question:
Let $I_n=\displaystyle\int_1^ex(\ln x)^n\,dx$ for integers $n\ge1$, and suppose $I_{n+1}=\dfrac12e^2-\dfrac12(n+1)I_n$ for $n\ge0$.

Prove by induction that for all positive integers $n$, $I_n$ is of the form $A_ne^2+B_n$, where $A_n$ and $B_n$ are rational numbers.
questions.answer:
*Base case $n=1$:* $I_0=\displaystyle\int_1^ex\,dx=\dfrac{e^2-1}2$, so $I_1=\dfrac{e^2}2-\dfrac12I_0=\dfrac{e^2}2-\dfrac{e^2-1}4=\dfrac14e^2+\dfrac14$. So $A_1=B_1=\tfrac14$ are rational.

*Inductive step:* assume $I_n=A_ne^2+B_n$ with $A_n,B_n\in\mathbb{Q}$ for some $n\ge1$. Then
$$I_{n+1}=\frac{e^2}2-\frac{n+1}2\left(A_ne^2+B_n\right)=\underbrace{\tfrac12\bigl(1-(n+1)A_n\bigr)}_{A_{n+1}}e^2+\underbrace{\left(-\tfrac12(n+1)B_n\right)}_{B_{n+1}}.$$
Since $A_n,B_n$ are rational, so are $A_{n+1}$ and $B_{n+1}$. So the statement holds for $n+1$ whenever it holds for $n$.

By mathematical induction it holds for all positive integers $n$. $\blacksquare$

questions.question:
Two blocks are not attached to each other. The larger block has mass $M=88$ kg and the smaller block has mass $m=16$ kg. A horizontal force $\vec F$ pushes the smaller block against the vertical face of the larger block, as shown. The coefficient of static friction between the blocks is $\mu=0.38$, but the surface beneath the larger block is frictionless.

What is the minimum magnitude of the horizontal force required to keep the smaller block from slipping down the larger block? (Take $g=9.8\ \text{m s}^{-2}$ and give your answer to 2 significant figures.)
questions.answer:
Let $N$ be the normal reaction between the blocks and $a$ the common horizontal acceleration.

*Whole system (horizontal):* $F=(m+M)a$.
*Small block (vertical), on the point of slipping:* $\mu N=mg$, so $N=\dfrac{mg}\mu$.
*Large block (horizontal):* $N=Ma$.

Hence $a=\dfrac N M=\dfrac{mg}{\mu M}$ and
$$F=(m+M)\frac{mg}{\mu M}=\frac{16\times9.8\times(16+88)}{0.38\times88}\approx488\ \text{N}\approx490\ \text{N}.$$
(The paper's intermediate formula omitted the $M$ in the denominator, but its numerical working used it correctly.)

questions.question:
It is known that for positive numbers $a,b,c$ the arithmetic mean is at least the geometric mean: $\dfrac{a+b+c}3\ge\sqrt[3]{abc}$.

Given $a+b+c=t$ and $a,b,c>0$, prove that $\dfrac1a+\dfrac1b+\dfrac1c\ge\dfrac9t$.
questions.answer:
From the given inequality, $\sqrt[3]{abc}\le\dfrac t3$, so $\dfrac1{\sqrt[3]{abc}}\ge\dfrac3t$.

Apply AM–GM to the positive numbers $\dfrac1a,\dfrac1b,\dfrac1c$:
$$\frac1a+\frac1b+\frac1c\ge3\sqrt[3]{\frac1a\cdot\frac1b\cdot\frac1c}=\frac3{\sqrt[3]{abc}}\ge3\cdot\frac3t=\frac9t.\ \blacksquare$$

questions.question: Given $a,b,c>0$ and $a+b+c=1$, prove that $\left(\dfrac1a-1\right)\left(\dfrac1b-1\right)\left(\dfrac1c-1\right)\ge8$. (You may use the result that $\dfrac1a+\dfrac1b+\dfrac1c\ge\dfrac9{a+b+c}$ for positive $a,b,c$.)
questions.answer:
Expand:
$$\left(\frac1a-1\right)\left(\frac1b-1\right)\left(\frac1c-1\right)=\frac1{abc}-\frac{a+b+c}{abc}+\frac1a+\frac1b+\frac1c-1.$$
(using $\dfrac1{ab}+\dfrac1{bc}+\dfrac1{ca}=\dfrac{a+b+c}{abc}$.) Since $a+b+c=1$, the first two terms cancel and the product equals $\dfrac1a+\dfrac1b+\dfrac1c-1$.

By the given result with $t=1$, $\dfrac1a+\dfrac1b+\dfrac1c\ge9$, so the product is at least $9-1=8$. $\blacksquare$

questions.question:
A drone $A$ of mass $1$ kg moves under gravity and air resistance. The resistive force is proportional to its velocity, $F=-kv$ with $k>0$, and the acceleration due to gravity is $g>0$. Drone $A$ is launched vertically upward from ground level (take its initial position as the origin) with initial speed $U$ m/s.

Show that the height of $A$ at time $t$ is $y_A=\left(\dfrac{kU+g}{k^2}\right)\left(1-e^{-kt}\right)-\dfrac{gt}k$.
questions.answer:
Taking upward as positive, $\ddot y=-g-kv$, i.e. $\dfrac{dv}{dt}=-(g+kv)$. Separating variables,
$$\int\frac{dv}{g+kv}=-\int dt\ \Rightarrow\ \frac1k\ln(g+kv)=-t+C_1.$$
At $t=0$, $v=U$, so $g+kv=(g+kU)e^{-kt}$ and
$$v=\left(U+\frac gk\right)e^{-kt}-\frac gk.$$
Integrating, $y=-\dfrac1k\left(U+\dfrac gk\right)e^{-kt}-\dfrac{g}{k}t+C$. With $y=0$ at $t=0$, $C=\dfrac{kU+g}{k^2}$, so
$$y_A=\frac{kU+g}{k^2}\left(1-e^{-kt}\right)-\frac{gt}k.\ \blacksquare$$

questions.question:
Two drones $A$ and $B$, each of mass $1$ kg, move under gravity and air resistance. The resistive force on each drone is $-k\mathbf v$ (proportional to its velocity, $k>0$) and $g>0$ is the acceleration due to gravity.

At time $t=0$, drone $A$ is launched vertically upward from the origin $(0,0)$ with speed $U$ m/s, so that its height is $y_A=\dfrac{kU+g}{k^2}\left(1-e^{-kt}\right)-\dfrac{gt}k$. At the same time drone $B$ starts at height $H$ m, a horizontal distance $d$ m from $A$ (at position $(-d,H)$), moving horizontally towards $A$ with initial speed $V$ m/s and no initial vertical velocity.

Find $d$ in terms of $U$, $V$, $k$ and $H$ so that the two drones collide, and explain why $V>kd$.
questions.answer:
*Motion of $B$.* Horizontally, $\ddot x=-k\dot x$, so $\dot x=Ve^{-kt}$ and $x=-\dfrac Vke^{-kt}+C$; with $x=-d$ at $t=0$, $C=\dfrac Vk-d$:
$$x_B=\frac Vk\left(1-e^{-kt}\right)-d.$$
Vertically, $\ddot y=-g-k\dot y$ with $\dot y=0$ initially gives $\dot y=\dfrac gk\left(e^{-kt}-1\right)$, and with $y=H$ at $t=0$,
$$y_B=H-\frac gkt+\frac g{k^2}\left(1-e^{-kt}\right).$$

*Collision.* Drone $A$ stays on the line $x=0$, so we need $x_B=0$ and $y_A=y_B$ at the same time $t$.

From $x_B=0$: $\dfrac Vk(1-e^{-kt})=d$, so $1-e^{-kt}=\dfrac{kd}V$. $\quad(1)$

From $y_A=y_B$:
$$\frac{kU+g}{k^2}(1-e^{-kt})-\frac{gt}k=H-\frac{gt}k+\frac g{k^2}(1-e^{-kt})\ \Rightarrow\ \frac Uk\left(1-e^{-kt}\right)=H.\quad(2)$$

Substituting (1) into (2): $\dfrac Uk\cdot\dfrac{kd}V=H$, so
$$d=\frac{VH}{U}.$$
(The answer does not depend on $k$.)

*Why $V>kd$.* From (1), $e^{-kt}=1-\dfrac{kd}V$. Since $e^{-kt}>0$ for all real $t$, we need $1-\dfrac{kd}V>0$, i.e. $V>kd$. Physically, $B$'s horizontal distance travelled tends to the limit $\dfrac Vk$ (its terminal horizontal extent), so $B$ can only reach $x=0$ if $d<\dfrac Vk$.

(Note: the printed paper omitted part (ii), which in the school's solutions is finding the position of $B$; it is included in the working above.)
